summary: Describes a framework for making Integrated Services, which reserve resources for individual flows, work across networks that use Differentiated Services, which treat traffic by class. It explains how reservations made at the edges can be honored across a Diffserv region. It is informational guidance, not a protocol specification.

eli5.summary: Some roads let you book a lane just for your car, while others only have a bus lane for everyone. This explains how to make a trip work smoothly across both kinds of roads.

questions: how do intserv and diffserv work together
what is admission control in qos
what is a service level specification
subtitle: How per-flow reservations made with RSVP can work end to end across a Diffserv network that only treats traffic by class.

tldr.problem: Intserv with RSVP lets applications reserve resources for individual flows, but per-flow state scales poorly. Diffserv scales well because it handles a few aggregate classes, but it has no signaling to admit or reject individual requests.
tldr.mechanism: Treat each Diffserv region as one virtual link inside an Intserv network. RSVP messages cross the region, edge or border routers act as admission control agents, and the Intserv service is mapped to a Diffserv PHB, with policing at the region's edge.
tldr.outcome: The framework describes statically provisioned, RSVP-aware and oracle-driven regions, the requirements they must meet, and open multicast problems. It is guidance, not a protocol specification.

facts.value: Tx, ER1, BR1, BR2, ER2, Rx

today: RFC 2998 is an Informational memo from November 2000, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes a framework, not a protocol, and several mechanisms it relies on were still described as work in progress when it was written.

sections.title: Intserv, RSVP and Diffserv
sections.content:
The Integrated Services (Intserv) architecture aims to give applications end-to-end QoS. Its services are controlled load and guaranteed service, and it assumes an explicit setup mechanism, of which RSVP is the best known. RSVP signals per-flow needs, and network elements admit or reject requests and configure microflow (MF) classifiers that use IP addresses and port numbers. The RFC lists three obstacles to deploying RSVP widely: per-flow state and processing raise scalability concerns, only a small number of hosts generate RSVP signaling, and the needed policy control mechanisms (access control, authentication, accounting) had only recently become available.

Differentiated Services (Diffserv) instead sorts packets into a small number of classes using the Diffserv codepoint (DSCP). Each router applies a per-hop behavior (PHB) invoked by the DSCP. This is behavior aggregate (BA) classification, and its main benefit is scalability.

The framework treats them as complementary. Intserv lets hosts ask for quantifiable resources and get feedback on admissibility, while Diffserv gives scalability across large networks. A Diffserv region is a set of contiguous routers that do BA classification and traffic control. From Intserv's point of view it is a virtual link connecting Intserv-capable routers or hosts.
sections.eli5: Intserv is like booking a seat for each person, which is precise but hard to do for a huge crowd. Diffserv is like sorting people into a few lines, which is easy for a crowd but gives no promises. The idea is to use both.

sections.title: Why Combine Them
sections.content:
Diffserv alone applies admission control statically, by provisioning policing parameters. The RFC gives an example: an ingress element set to accept only 50 Kbps of EF traffic, with 10 IP telephony sessions of 10 Kbps each, will discard half the offered traffic with no regard to which microflow it came from. Likely none of the ten sessions gets satisfactory service, even though resources exist for five. With explicit signaling, requests beyond the limit are rejected, so hosts and applications can back off, ask for less, mark traffic best effort, or reroute, and the admitted flows are preserved.

Other benefits listed are:

  • Policy-based admission control: RSVP requests identify the user and application, so per-user or per-application policy can apply instead of only per-customer-network policy.
  • Marking help: either hosts mark the DSCP, which scales best and works even when IPsec hides port numbers, or routers mark it using MF classification, which is hard to configure statically because of DHCP and transient ports. RSVP signaling can supply the needed information.
  • Traffic conditioning: Intserv-capable elements can shape or police per flow before traffic enters the Diffserv region.
sections.eli5: If a lane only fits five cars and ten show up, everyone gets squeezed and nobody gets through well. If cars ask first, five get in and the rest are told to wait or take another way.

sections.title: The Reference Network and Service Mapping
sections.content:
The reference network is a sender Tx and receiver Rx, each in a non-Diffserv region, with a Diffserv region in the middle. Edge routers (ER1, ER2) sit next to the Diffserv region and border routers (BR1, BR2) sit inside it. End-to-end RSVP messages must at least be carried across the Diffserv region, and routers there that are not RSVP aware pass them transparently.

If the Diffserv region is RSVP unaware, the edge routers act as admission control agents using the region's resource availability and customer policy, and the border routers just police traffic. If it is RSVP aware, the border routers act as the admission control agents.

Service mapping turns an Intserv request (a service type plus a flowspec) into something the region can provide: choosing a PHB, policing at the edges, exporting Intserv parameters such as ADSPEC updates, and doing admission control. The DSCP can follow a default mapping from Intserv service type, or a network driven mapping where RSVP-aware routers override it, communicated upstream with RSVP.

Aggregate policing at the border cannot stop one misbehaving microflow from taking more than its share. The RFC offers three fixes: per-microflow policing at the edge routers (generally the most appropriate), at the border routers (less scalable), or relying on trusted upstream shaping, possibly with some over-provisioning.
sections.eli5: The trip goes from a sender, through a gate, across the big sorted-lanes road, through another gate, to the receiver. The gates decide who may enter and which lane they use.

sections.title: A Statically Provisioned Diffserv Region
sections.content:
In the first example no device in the Diffserv region is RSVP aware. The customer and the region owner have negotiated a static service level specification (SLS) giving transmit capacity at each Diffserv service level, which may be just bandwidth or a richer profile with burst size, peak rate or time of day. Each customer edge router has an Intserv half and a Diffserv half, and keeps a table of provisioned capacity per service level.

The sequence runs as follows. Tx sends an RSVP PATH message toward Rx, and ER1 installs PATH state. Routers in the Diffserv region ignore it. Rx answers with a RESV message, which ER2 may reject if its downstream resources are insufficient. When RESV reaches ER1, ER1 compares the request to the capacity left at the mapped service level, and may also reject it on customer policy. If approved, ER1 reduces its table of available capacity and passes RESV upstream. Tx treats receipt of RESV as admission, learns the DSCP from the default mapping or from the RESV, and may mark packets with it.

The RFC notes that this setup cannot easily follow a changing SLS, because ER1 needs reconfiguring, and that admission control ignores the resources on the specific path.
sections.eli5: You send a note ahead asking for a seat. The receiver says yes. The first gate checks its list of free seats in the big road, crosses one off, and passes the yes back to you.

sections.title: RSVP-Aware Regions, Oracles and Multicast
sections.content:
In the second example the region is RSVP aware: its control plane is RSVP but its data plane is Diffserv. This gives topology aware admission control, since the agent knows resources along the specific path, and lets the region adjust provisioning (for example the bandwidth given to the EF queue) in response to requests. The options are:

  • Aggregated or tunneled RSVP: border and core routers reserve resources for aggregates between region edges. It needs less signaling processing than per-flow RSVP and is most likely feasible only in one administrative domain.
  • Per-flow RSVP: routers in the region respond to ordinary per-flow signaling. It uses resources more efficiently, but puts higher demands on signaling.
  • Oracle or bandwidth broker: border routers use custom protocols to ask an agent that knows resource availability and topology.

How many core routers take part in RSVP is a provisioning choice. At one extreme only border routers do, which needs heavy over-provisioning or careful static provisioning, and at the other every router does, which is the most efficient but has the most overhead.

The RFC requires that a Diffserv region support standard Intserv services between its border routers using standard PHBs, provide admission control information to its customers, and pass RSVP messages so they can be recovered at the egress. It also says Intserv traffic, non-Intserv traffic and best effort traffic must be isolated, and suggests the DSCPs for Intserv traffic should not overlap with others.

Multicast is significantly more complex. Where receivers need different service, a branch point core router that only does BA classification cannot easily demote packets on the unreserved branch. The RFC lists several partial remedies, none ideal in all cases, and notes that writing meaningful SLSs for heterogeneous multicast flows is likely to be challenging.
sections.eli5: The big road can either stay fixed, or it can listen to requests and change how much room each lane gets. Listening works better but takes more effort, and shared rides (multicast) make it trickier.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because RSVP signaling is used in both Diffserv and non-Diffserv regions, all RSVP security considerations apply, and administrators are expected to configure secure policers at interfaces with untrusted customers.

The framework does not require host marking of the DSCP but allows it, which may alarm administrators who fear hosts will steal resources. Hosts could exceed their negotiated capacity whether they set the DSCP directly or send traffic that a marking router classifies into a given DSCP, so each Diffserv region should police at every service level. The exception is a host known to be trusted, such as a server under the control of the network administrator.
sections.eli5: Anyone could claim they deserve the fast lane, so the gate must check that each customer only uses the share they were given.

items.text: Border routers ask an agent, such as a bandwidth broker, about resources.
